name: Feldenkrais Method

lead: The Feldenkrais Method is a movement-education system created by Moshe Feldenkrais (1904-1984). It is taught in verbally guided group classes (Awareness Through Movement) and one-to-one hands-on sessions (Functional Integration).

Proponents say it improves awareness and ease of movement, and it is sometimes mentioned in posture discussions. Reviews describe no conclusive evidence of medical benefit, with some small trials in chronic low back pain; no study found tests it for appearance.

paras: Proponents say slow, exploratory movement and attention to sensation help the nervous system learn new movement patterns. Some researchers link the method to dynamic systems theory of motor behaviour.

Wikipedia says researchers do not believe the method poses serious risks. Critics, including physician David Gorski, have compared it to faith healing, and Australian government review found no clear evidence of effectiveness.

lead: The Feldenkrais Method is a form of somatic education devised by Israeli physicist and judo expert Moshe Feldenkrais (1904-1984). Its two formats are Awareness Through Movement, verbally guided group lessons, and Functional Integration, hands-on individual sessions.[1][2] Proponents claim it improves movement quality and awareness and repairs brain-body connections.[2]

Reviews report no conclusive evidence of medical benefit. A 2015 Australian government review found no clear evidence of effectiveness and in 2017 it was excluded from private health insurance subsidies, according to Wikipedia.[2] Small randomised trials in chronic low back pain exist, and systematic reviews have assessed its use as a physiotherapy tool.[3][4][5] No study found tests it for posture appearance.

paras: Feldenkrais was born in Slavuta and studied engineering and physics in Paris, where he practised judo. After a knee injury in 1940s Britain, he experimented with gentle movement. He published Body and Mature Behaviour in 1949 and taught in Tel Aviv from the early 1950s.[1] He taught practitioners in San Francisco and Amherst trainings, and the International Feldenkrais Federation was founded in 1994.[1][2]

A 2017 single-blind randomised trial of 53 patients with chronic low back pain compared the method with Back School for pain and interoceptive awareness, and a 2020 randomised trial compared it with core stability exercise.[6][7] A 1999 controlled study examined Feldenkrais bodywork versus sham in multiple sclerosis.[8]

A 2015 systematic review and a 2022 systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials assessed its effectiveness as a physiotherapy tool.[4][5] A 2022 German IQWiG report, per Wikipedia, found a hint of benefit in Parkinson disease and inconsistent results for chronic low back pain without long-term benefit evidence.[2] No studies found testing posture appearance as an outcome.

David Gorski has described the method as borders on quackery and compared it to faith healing, and Quackwatch lists it among unnaturalistic methods, as summarised on Wikipedia.[2] A review of bodywork trial methodology discusses bias control in this research area.[9]

timeline.event: Feldenkrais publishes Body and Mature Behaviour.[1]
First US professional training begins in San Francisco.[1]
